change_thresholds.label: distribution-based estimate, not an MCID
change_thresholds.note: MCID / MID cannot be computed by this software. A minimal clinically important difference is the smallest change that users, clinicians or caregivers judge to be important; establishing it requires ANCHOR-BASED evidence from real participants - e.g. a global rating of change, a patient-reported or clinician-rated functional anchor, or achievement of a meaningful real-world goal - linked to observed score changes (Revicki et al. 2008; de Vet & Terwee 2010) [PK]. It cannot be derived from simulated users, from the score distribution alone, or from reliability statistics: the minimal detectable change (MDC) says what change exceeds measurement noise (statistically detectable), not what change matters (clinically important). Distribution-based quantities (0.5 SD, 1 SEM, MDC) are reported only as 'distribution-based estimate, not an MCID' and may be used as supportive evidence to triangulate anchor-based estimates in a future participant study.

icc.method: two-way ANOVA mean squares; ICC per Shrout & Fleiss (1979) / McGraw & Wong (1996); 95% CI F-based (McGraw & Wong 1996); agreement forms also get a generalized CI (gci_low/gci_high, 10000 draws, seed 0)
assumptions: scores are interval-scaled and approximately normal
subject and error effects independent; homoscedastic error
no subject x session interaction (two-way models)
sessions treated as random (A forms, ICC(1)) or fixed (C forms)

sem_mdc.method: SEM from two-way ANOVA; MDC = z*sqrt(2)*SEM
assumptions: homoscedastic measurement error (same SEM at all score levels)
normally distributed error (for the z multipliers)

bland_altman.method: Bland-Altman (1986, 1999): bias, LoA = bias +/- z*SD(d), LoA CI method 'ba1999'; proportional bias by OLS of d on mean
assumptions: one independent pair per subject
differences approx. normal
bias and SD of differences constant over the measurement range

lin_ccc.method: Lin (1989) CCC, 1/n moments; Fisher-z CI with Lin's asymptotic variance
assumptions: paired continuous measurements
approx. bivariate normal

agreement.note: differences are session2 - session1 (positive = higher at retest)

change_over_sessions.method: linear mixed model (REML), statsmodels MixedLM; Wald CIs for fixed effects
assumptions: normal random effects and residuals
missing at random (MAR)
linear time trend
homoscedastic residuals, conditional independence given random effects

floor_ceiling.method: proportion at bound; flag > threshold (Terwee et al. 2007)
assumptions: bounds are the true scale limits

internal_consistency.reason: Internal-consistency coefficients (Cronbach alpha, McDonald omega) are only meaningful for a set of items that are intended to measure ONE construct (a reflective, unidimensional scale, e.g. the items of a questionnaire). They are NOT appropriate for an arbitrary set of task metrics (e.g. throughput, error rate, path efficiency, latency): such metrics are formative/heterogeneous, may legitimately be uncorrelated, and a low or high alpha says nothing about the reliability of any single metric. Use test-retest ICC for task metrics.

psychometrics.invariance_scope: Formal measurement invariance (multi-group confirmatory factor analysis testing configural, metric/weak, scalar/strong and strict invariance; Meredith 1993; Vandenberg & Lance 2000) and differential item functioning are OUT OF SCOPE for v1 because: (1) NeuroMetric task scores are single observed metrics, not multiple reflective indicators of one latent factor, so a factor model per group is not identified or not meaningful; (2) multi-group CFA needs several hundred participants per group for stable estimates, far beyond the planned pilot samples; (3) no CFA/SEM engine is among the vetted dependencies. v1 therefore checks the observable consequences that matter for using a score across input modalities: equal reliability (ICC difference with bootstrap CI) and equivalent means within a pre-specified margin (TOST). Neither establishes that the score measures the same construct in each group; that requires construct-validity evidence per group.
